topic: Classes: data, sealed, object, enum & delegation

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `copy` creates a new object with the given properties changed and leaves the original untouched, so `u.age` is still 30. `v` keeps the name "Ann". The generated `equals` compares every constructor property, and the ages differ, so the result is false.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of modeling screen state as a `sealed interface` instead of an open interface?
options: Sealed subtypes get `equals`, `hashCode` and `copy` generated, like data classes
Sealed types can be used across modules, while open interfaces are limited to one module
The compiler knows every subtype, so `when` can be exhaustive and breaks when a new state is added
Sealed types are allocated once and cached, which makes state updates cheaper than with an open interface
questions.explanation: All direct subtypes of a sealed type are known at compile time, so a `when` over it can be checked for exhaustiveness. Adding a new state then shows a compile error at every `when` that does not handle it, instead of silently falling into `else`. Sealed types do not generate data-class members, and their subtypes must stay in the same module and package.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Generated `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` and `copy` only use properties declared in the primary constructor. `label` is in the class body, so it is ignored: the two points are equal and `toString` does not show it. This can hide real differences, and `copy()` silently resets such properties.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `Loud` overrides `greet()`, so `l.greet()` is "HI". `twice()` is not overridden, so it is forwarded to the delegate `b`, and inside `b` the call to `greet()` goes to `Base.greet()`. Delegation is not inheritance: the delegate never sees the wrapper's overrides.

questions.question: An `object` declaration is initialized lazily, on first access, and that initialization is thread-safe on the JVM.
questions.explanation: An `object` compiles to a class with a static instance created in its static initializer. The JVM runs that initializer on first use of the class and guarantees it runs only once, even with concurrent access. That is why `object` is a simple, safe singleton without double-checked locking.

questions.question: Which members does the compiler generate for a data class from its primary constructor properties? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A data class gets `equals`/`hashCode`, `toString`, `copy` and `componentN` functions for destructuring. It does not implement `Comparable`, so there is no `compareTo`. A no-argument constructor only exists if every parameter has a default value (or via a compiler plugin).

questions.question: Why is `data object Loading : UiState` usually preferred over `object Loading : UiState` in a sealed state hierarchy?
options: It creates a new instance each time it is used, so state flows always emit a new value
It is the only kind of object allowed as a subtype of a sealed interface
Its `toString()` prints `Loading` instead of a class name plus hash, so logs are readable
It allows `copy()`, so the state can be updated in the same way as the other data-class states
questions.explanation: A `data object` is still a singleton, but it gets a readable `toString()` (`Loading`) and matching `equals`/`hashCode`. A plain object prints something like `Loading@1b6d3586`, which is noise in logs and test failures. It has no `copy()` because it has no properties.

questions.question: What is the default thread-safety mode of `by lazy { }`, and when is `LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE` a reasonable choice?
options: Default is NONE; SYNCHRONIZED should be used only when the value is a mutable object
Default is SYNCHRONIZED; NONE lets several threads read the value without the initializer ever running twice
Default is SYNCHRONIZED; NONE skips locking and is safe only when the property is used from a single thread
Default is PUBLICATION; NONE is the same mode but also lets the initializer run more than once
questions.explanation: By default `lazy` uses a lock so the initializer runs exactly once even with concurrent access. `NONE` removes the lock, which saves a little overhead but can run the initializer twice or expose a partly built value under concurrency. It fits values only touched on the main thread. `PUBLICATION` allows the initializer to run more than once but makes all threads use the first stored value.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
data class Key(var id: Int)

fun main() {
    val set = hashSetOf(Key(1))
    val k = set.first()
    k.id = 2
    println("${set.contains(k)} ${set.contains(Key(1))} ${set.size}")
}
questions.explanation: The element was stored in the bucket for hash 1. After `id` changes to 2, `contains(k)` looks in the bucket for hash 2 and finds nothing. `contains(Key(1))` finds the right bucket, but `equals` compares it with an element whose id is now 2, so it also fails. The element is still there (size 1) but can no longer be found, which is why data-class keys should be immutable.

questions.question: When is a sealed hierarchy a better fit than an enum class?
options: When each case must be a singleton that can be compared with `==`
When cases carry different data, like `Error(val message: String)` next to `Loading`
When you need to iterate over every possible case at runtime, for example with `entries`
When all cases need a shared property, such as a display label or an icon for each one
questions.explanation: Each enum constant is a single instance with the same set of properties, so it cannot carry per-use data like an error message. Sealed subtypes can be data classes with their own fields, or objects when there is no data. Iterating over `entries`, singleton cases, and shared properties are all things enums already do well.
